sn.s: Die Beteiligung liegt oft bei ungefähr fünfundvierzig Prozent.
sn.e: The turnout is often at about forty-five per cent.

sn.s: Das ist wenig und alle finden es zu wenig und es ändert sich nicht.
sn.e: That is low and everybody finds it too low and it does not change.

sn.s: Ich habe Marco gefragt, ob er immer abstimmt.
sn.e: I asked Marco whether he always votes.

sn.s: Er hat gesagt: Meistens.
sn.e: He said: mostly.

sn.s: Er hat gesagt: Bei manchen Sachen finde ich, dass ich zu wenig weiss.
sn.e: He said: with some things I find that I know too little.

sn.s: Er hat gesagt: Dann lasse ich es.
sn.e: He said: then I leave it.

sn.s: Er hat das ohne schlechtes Gewissen gesagt und es hat mich überrascht.
sn.e: He said that without a bad conscience and it surprised me.

sn.s: Selina macht es anders und sie macht es am Küchentisch, laut.
sn.e: Selina does it differently and she does it at the kitchen table, out loud.

sn.s: Sie liest die zwei Seiten im Heft und sie redet dabei mit sich.
sn.e: She reads the two pages in the booklet and talks to herself while she does.

sn.s: Dann macht sie ein Kreuz und dann ist es fertig.
sn.e: Then she makes a cross and then it is done.

sn.s: Sie hat mich zweimal gefragt, was ich davon halte.
sn.e: She has twice asked me what I think about it.

sn.s: Das erste Mal habe ich gesagt, dass ich nichts sagen sollte.
sn.e: The first time I said that I should not say anything.

sn.s: Sie hat gesagt: Warum nicht?
sn.e: She said: why not?

sn.s: Ich habe gesagt: Weil ich nicht abstimmen darf.
sn.e: I said: because I am not allowed to vote.

sn.s: Sie hat gesagt: Du wohnst hier. Es betrifft dich auch.
sn.e: She said: you live here. It concerns you too.

sn.s: Sie hat recht und es ist trotzdem komisch.
sn.e: She is right and it is still odd.

sn.s: Ich lebe seit drei Jahren in einem Land, in dem ich nichts entscheiden kann.
sn.e: I have lived for three years in a country where I cannot decide anything.

sn.s: Das ist normal für sehr viele Leute hier.
sn.e: That is normal for a great many people here.

sn.s: Ungefähr ein Viertel von den Erwachsenen darf nicht abstimmen.
sn.e: About a quarter of the adults are not allowed to vote.

sn.s: Ein Viertel ist eine sehr grosse Zahl für ein Land, das über alles abstimmt.
sn.e: A quarter is a very large number for a country that votes on everything.

sn.s: Nuno ist achtzehn Jahre hier und darf nicht.
sn.e: Nuno has been here eighteen years and is not allowed to.

sn.s: Er redet nie darüber und ich habe ihn einmal gefragt.
sn.e: He never talks about it and I asked him once.

sn.s: Er hat gesagt: Meine Kinder dürfen. Das reicht mir.
sn.e: He said: my children are allowed to. That is enough for me.

sn.s: Er hat es schnell gesagt und dann über etwas anderes geredet.
sn.e: He said it quickly and then talked about something else.

sn.s: Ich glaube nicht, dass es ihm reicht.
sn.e: I do not think that it is enough for him.

sn.s: Fatlum darf und er sagt, dass er jedes Mal abstimmt.
sn.e: Fatlum is allowed to and he says that he votes every time.

sn.s: Er hat gesagt: Ich habe zwölf Jahre darauf gewartet.
sn.e: He said: I waited twelve years for it.

sn.s: Er hat gesagt: Ich lasse keine aus.
sn.e: He said: I do not miss a single one.

sn.s: Er hat gesagt: Auch die dummen nicht.
sn.e: He said: not even the stupid ones.

sn.s: Es gibt einen Satz, der an diesen Sonntagen oft fällt.
sn.e: There is a sentence that is often said on those Sundays.

sn.s: Man sagt: Das Volk hat entschieden.
sn.e: People say: the people have decided.

sn.s: Man sagt es auch, wenn man verloren hat, und man sagt es ruhig.
sn.e: You say it even when you have lost, and you say it calmly.

sn.s: Das ist die eigentliche Sache an dem ganzen System.
sn.e: That is the real thing about the whole system.

sn.s: Es ist nicht, dass alle mitentscheiden.
sn.e: It is not that everybody decides.

sn.s: Es ist, dass alle das Resultat annehmen, auch wenn es knapp ist.
sn.e: It is that everybody accepts the result, even when it is close.

sn.s: Im Februar ist eine Sache mit einem Prozent Unterschied entschieden worden.
sn.e: In February something was decided by one per cent.

sn.s: Am Montag im Büro hat niemand ein Wort darüber gesagt.
sn.e: On Monday in the office nobody said a word about it.

sn.s: Ich habe zwei Leute gefragt, wie sie gestimmt haben.
sn.e: I asked two people how they had voted.

sn.s: Beide haben es mir gesagt und beide haben nicht gefragt, was ich denke.
sn.e: Both told me and neither asked what I think.

sn.s: Das war die höflichste Antwort auf eine Frage, die ich nicht hätte stellen sollen.
sn.e: That was the politest answer to a question I should not have asked.

sn.s: Man fragt hier nicht, wie jemand gestimmt hat.
sn.e: You do not ask here how somebody voted.

sn.s: Das habe ich erst danach gelernt und niemand hat es mir gesagt.
sn.e: I only learnt that afterwards and nobody told me.

sn.s: Selina hat gelacht, als ich es ihr erzählt habe.
sn.e: Selina laughed when I told her about it.

sn.s: Sie hat gesagt: Und, haben sie geantwortet?
sn.e: She said: and, did they answer?

sn.s: Ich habe gesagt: Beide.
sn.e: I said: both of them.

sn.s: Sie hat gesagt: Dann mögen sie dich.
sn.e: She said: then they like you.

lessons.title: Eine Meinung, locker gehalten
lessons.desc: Having a view without insisting on it

sn.s: Ich habe im Oktober einen Satz flach in einen Tisch gelegt.
sn.e: In October I put a sentence flat down onto a table.

sn.s: Wir waren zu sechst und es ist um eine Sache aus der Zeitung gegangen.
sn.e: There were six of us and it was about something from the newspaper.

sn.s: Ich habe gesagt: Das ist falsch.
sn.e: I said: that is wrong.

sn.s: Drei Wörter, ohne alles.
sn.e: Three words, with nothing on them.

sn.s: Man hat gesehen, wie sich der Tisch bewegt.
sn.e: You could see the table shift.

sn.s: Niemand hat widersprochen und niemand hat zugestimmt.
sn.e: Nobody contradicted and nobody agreed.

sn.s: Zwei Leute haben gleichzeitig etwas Kleines gesagt.
sn.e: Two people said something small at the same time.

sn.s: Einer hat gesagt: Ja, man kann es so sehen.
sn.e: One said: yes, you can see it that way.

sn.s: Der andere hat gesagt: Es ist halt kompliziert.
sn.e: The other said: it is complicated, though.

sn.s: Beide Sätze heissen: mach das kleiner.
sn.e: Both sentences mean: make that smaller.

sn.s: Das Problem war nicht die Meinung.
sn.e: The problem was not the opinion.

sn.s: Alle am Tisch haben ungefähr das Gleiche gedacht.
sn.e: Everybody at the table thought roughly the same.

sn.s: Das Problem war die Form.
sn.e: The problem was the form.

sn.s: Eine Meinung wird hier nicht flach hingelegt.
sn.e: An opinion is not put down flat here.

sn.s: Man legt sie hin und lässt sie ein bisschen offen.
sn.e: You put it down and leave it a little open.

sn.s: Es gibt dafür ein paar feste Anfänge und sie sind alle gleich lang.
sn.e: There are a few fixed openings for it and they are all the same length.

sn.s: Ich finde eigentlich.
sn.e: I actually find.

sn.s: Mir scheint.
sn.e: It seems to me.

sn.s: Ich habe den Eindruck.
sn.e: I have the impression.

sn.s: Für mich ist es so, dass.
sn.e: For me it is the case that.

sn.s: Alle vier sagen das Gleiche und alle vier sagen: das ist meines.
sn.e: All four say the same thing and all four say: this is mine.

sn.s: Sie sagen nicht: das ist so.
sn.e: They do not say: that is how it is.

sn.s: Der Unterschied ist klein und er ist die ganze Sache.
sn.e: The difference is small and it is the whole thing.

sn.s: Wer sagt, dass etwas so ist, hat es für alle entschieden.
sn.e: Whoever says that something is so has decided it for everybody.

sn.s: Wer sagt, dass er es so findet, hat nur für sich geredet.
sn.e: Whoever says that they find it so has only spoken for themselves.

sn.s: Und dann können die anderen etwas dazulegen, ohne zu streiten.
sn.e: And then the others can add something without arguing.

sn.s: Ich habe zuerst gedacht, dass das Angst ist.
sn.e: At first I thought that this was fear.

sn.s: Ich habe gedacht: Sie trauen sich nicht, etwas zu sagen.
sn.e: I thought: they do not dare to say anything.

sn.s: Das ist falsch und ich habe ein Jahr gebraucht, um es zu sehen.
sn.e: That is wrong and it took me a year to see it.

sn.s: Sie sagen sehr viel und sie sagen es sehr direkt.
sn.e: They say a great deal and they say it very directly.

sn.s: Sie sagen es nur nicht als letztes Wort.
sn.e: They just do not say it as the last word.

sn.s: Ein Gespräch ist hier kein Wettbewerb, den einer gewinnt.
sn.e: A conversation here is not a competition that somebody wins.

sn.s: Es ist ein Tisch, auf den alle etwas legen.
sn.e: It is a table on which everybody puts something.

sn.s: Wer am lautesten redet, spielt eine Rolle und das merken alle.
sn.e: Whoever talks loudest is playing a part and everybody notices.

sn.s: Am Schluss schaut man, was liegt, und meistens sind alle ungefähr einig.
sn.e: At the end you look at what is lying there, and mostly everybody roughly agrees.

sn.s: Das ganze Land wird so regiert und das ist keine Übertreibung.
sn.e: The whole country is governed like that and that is not an exaggeration.

sn.s: Es gibt sieben Leute in der Regierung, aus vier Parteien, die sich nicht mögen.
sn.e: There are seven people in the government, from four parties, who do not like each other.

sn.s: Sie streiten und dann kommen sie mit einem Entscheid heraus.
sn.e: They argue and then they come out with one decision.

sn.s: Danach sagen alle sieben das Gleiche, auch die, die dagegen waren.
sn.e: Afterwards all seven say the same thing, including the ones who were against.

sn.s: Von aussen tönt das falsch.
sn.e: From the outside that sounds false.

sn.s: Von innen ist es die Regel, ohne die es nicht funktionieren würde.
sn.e: From the inside it is the rule without which it would not work.

sn.s: Es hat eine Grenze und die habe ich falsch eingeschätzt.
sn.e: It has a limit and I misjudged it.

sn.s: Ich habe gedacht, dass hier niemand streitet.
sn.e: I thought that nobody argues here.

sn.s: Man streitet sehr wohl und man streitet über die Sache.
sn.e: People do argue and they argue about the matter.

sn.s: Man greift den Menschen nicht an und das ist der ganze Unterschied.
sn.e: You do not attack the person and that is the whole difference.

sn.s: Ich habe an einer Versammlung vom Verein zugeschaut.
sn.e: I watched at a club meeting.

sn.s: Es ist um sechshundert Franken gegangen und es hat vierzig Minuten gedauert.
sn.e: It was about six hundred francs and it lasted forty minutes.

sn.s: Zwei Männer haben sich ganz klar widersprochen.
sn.e: Two men contradicted each other quite clearly.

sn.s: Beide haben gesagt: Ich sehe das anders.
sn.e: Both said: I see that differently.

sn.s: Beide haben gesagt: Das kann ich nicht unterstützen.
sn.e: Both said: I cannot support that.

sn.s: Danach haben sie abgestimmt und einer hat verloren.
sn.e: Then they voted and one of them lost.

sn.s: Der, der verloren hat, hat das Protokoll geschrieben.
sn.e: The one who lost wrote the minutes.

sn.s: Zwanzig Minuten später sind sie zusammen etwas trinken gegangen.
sn.e: Twenty minutes later they went for a drink together.

sn.s: Das ist die Sache, die ich hier am meisten bewundere.
sn.e: That is the thing I most admire here.

sn.s: Man kann ganz genau sagen, dass man nicht einverstanden ist.
sn.e: You can say quite precisely that you disagree.

sn.s: Und es bleibt trotzdem eine Sache und wird keine Person.
sn.e: And it still stays a matter and does not become a person.

sn.s: Es gibt einen Satz, der das ganze Prinzip trägt.
sn.e: There is one sentence that carries the whole principle.

sn.s: Ich sehe das anders.
sn.e: I see that differently.

sn.s: Vier Wörter, sehr ruhig, und man kann sie überall sagen.
sn.e: Four words, very calmly, and you can say them anywhere.

sn.s: Sie greifen niemanden an und sie geben nichts auf.
sn.e: They attack nobody and they give up nothing.

sn.s: Ich habe sie im November zum ersten Mal gebraucht.
sn.e: I used them for the first time in November.

sn.s: Es ist im Büro um eine Sache gegangen, die ich falsch fand.
sn.e: It was about something in the office that I thought was wrong.

sn.s: Ich habe gesagt: Ich sehe das anders.
sn.e: I said: I see that differently.

sn.s: Und dann habe ich zwei Sätze gesagt, warum.
sn.e: And then I said two sentences about why.

sn.s: Simon hat gesagt: Gut, dann schauen wir das noch einmal an.
sn.e: Simon said: fine, then we will look at that again.

sn.s: Wir haben es nicht geändert.
sn.e: We did not change it.

sn.s: Und ich bin gehört worden und das ist etwas anderes.
sn.e: And I was heard and that is something else.

sn.s: Im Oktober, an dem Tisch mit sechs Leuten, habe ich es dann repariert.
sn.e: In October, at that table with six people, I then repaired it.

sn.s: Nicht sofort. Zehn Minuten später.
sn.e: Not immediately. Ten minutes later.

sn.s: Ich habe gesagt: Ich finde das eigentlich falsch, aber ich weiss zu wenig.
sn.e: I said: I actually find that wrong, but I know too little.

sn.s: Damit ist die Sache wieder auf den Tisch gekommen.
sn.e: With that the matter came back onto the table.

sn.s: Drei Leute haben etwas dazugelegt und dann waren wir eine halbe Stunde dran.
sn.e: Three people added something and then we were at it for half an hour.

sn.s: Am Schluss hat einer gesagt: Ja, im Grund hast du recht.
sn.e: At the end one of them said: yes, basically you are right.

sn.s: Er hat es leise gesagt und niemand hat es gross gemacht.
sn.e: He said it quietly and nobody made anything of it.

sn.s: Das ist hier ein Sieg und er tönt nach nichts.
sn.e: That is a victory here and it sounds like nothing.

lessons.title: Du tönst schon fast
lessons.desc: Somebody says you sound like one of them

sn.s: Nuno hat es im Dezember gesagt, in der Küche vom Restaurant.
sn.e: Nuno said it in December, in the restaurant kitchen.

sn.s: Er hat Zwiebeln geschnitten und nicht aufgeschaut.
sn.e: He was chopping onions and did not look up.

sn.s: Er hat gesagt: Du tönst schon fast wie einer von hier.
sn.e: He said: you already sound almost like one from here.

sn.s: Dann hat er weitergeschnitten.
sn.e: Then he went on chopping.

sn.s: Ich bin dort gestanden und habe nichts gesagt.
sn.e: I stood there and said nothing.

sn.s: Es sind acht Wörter und ich habe sie den ganzen Abend behalten.
sn.e: It is eight words and I kept them the whole evening.

sn.s: Ich habe sie immer noch.
sn.e: I still have them.

sn.s: Es ist wichtig, wer es gesagt hat.
sn.e: It matters who said it.

sn.s: Ein Schweizer hätte es nie so gesagt.
sn.e: A Swiss person would never have said it like that.

sn.s: Ein Schweizer sagt: Dein Deutsch ist gut geworden.
sn.e: A Swiss person says: your German has got good.

sn.s: Er sagt es freundlich und er meint es und es heisst etwas anderes.
sn.e: They say it kindly and they mean it and it means something else.

sn.s: Es heisst: du bist von aussen und du machst es gut.
sn.e: It means: you are from outside and you are doing it well.

sn.s: Nuno hat achtzehn Jahre gebraucht und er tönt immer noch nicht so.
sn.e: Nuno needed eighteen years and he still does not sound like that.

sn.s: Er weiss genau, was der Satz kostet.
sn.e: He knows exactly what the sentence costs.

sn.s: Darum wiegt er bei ihm mehr.
sn.e: That is why it weighs more from him.

sn.s: Das Wort ist tönen und es ist das Schweizer Wort dafür.
sn.e: The word is tönen and it is the Swiss word for it.

sn.s: Du tönst müde. Das tönt gut. Er tönt wie sein Vater.
sn.e: You sound tired. That sounds good. He sounds like his father.

sn.s: Schon fast heisst: noch nicht ganz und nicht mehr weit.
sn.e: Schon fast means: not quite yet and not far off.

sn.s: Es sind die zwei ehrlichsten Wörter in dem Satz.
sn.e: They are the two most honest words in the sentence.

sn.s: Ohne sie wäre der Satz zu gross und niemand hätte ihn geglaubt.
sn.e: Without them the sentence would be too big and nobody would have believed it.

sn.s: Ich habe zuerst nichts gesagt und das war Glück.
sn.e: At first I said nothing and that was luck.

sn.s: Man nimmt ein Lob hier nicht an.
sn.e: You do not accept praise here.

sn.s: Man wehrt es ab und der andere legt es noch einmal hin.
sn.e: You fend it off and the other person puts it down again.

sn.s: Die Wörter dafür sind kurz und man braucht sie oft.
sn.e: The words for it are short and you need them often.

sn.s: Ach was.
sn.e: Oh come on.

sn.s: Übertreib nicht.
sn.e: Do not exaggerate.

sn.s: Das ist noch weit.
sn.e: That is still a long way off.

sn.s: Ich mache immer noch viele Fehler.
sn.e: I still make a lot of mistakes.

sn.s: Alle vier sind richtig und alle vier sind das Gleiche.
sn.e: All four are correct and all four are the same thing.

sn.s: Man macht sich kleiner, damit der andere nicht zu viel gegeben hat.
sn.e: You make yourself smaller so that the other person has not given too much.

sn.s: Es gibt eine Grenze und sie ist da, wo es unehrlich wird.
sn.e: There is a limit and it is where it becomes dishonest.

sn.s: Wer sagt, dass er gar nichts kann, sagt dem anderen, dass er blind ist.
sn.e: Whoever says that they cannot do anything at all is telling the other person they are blind.

sn.s: Ich habe zu Nuno am Schluss etwas gesagt.
sn.e: In the end I said something to Nuno.

sn.s: Ich habe gesagt: Von dir zählt das mehr.
sn.e: I said: from you that counts for more.

sn.s: Er hat aufgeschaut und dann hat er gelacht.
sn.e: He looked up and then he laughed.

sn.s: Er hat gesagt: Ich weiss.
sn.e: He said: I know.

sn.s: Zwei Wörter und wir haben beide gewusst, worüber wir reden.
sn.e: Two words and we both knew what we were talking about.

sn.s: Der Satz ist selten und das ist der Grund, warum er zählt.
sn.e: The sentence is rare and that is the reason it counts.

sn.s: Ich habe ihn in drei Jahren zweimal gehört.
sn.e: I have heard it twice in three years.

sn.s: Das erste Mal von einer Frau im Zug, die es nicht so gemeint hat.
sn.e: The first time from a woman on a train, who did not mean it that way.

sn.s: Sie hat gefragt, aus welchem Kanton ich komme.
sn.e: She asked which canton I come from.

sn.s: Das war kein Lob, das war ein Missverständnis, und es hat trotzdem gut getan.
sn.e: That was not praise, that was a misunderstanding, and it still felt good.

sn.s: Das zweite Mal war Nuno, in einer Küche, über Zwiebeln.
sn.e: The second time was Nuno, in a kitchen, over onions.

sn.s: Man sagt es einem nicht zweimal.
sn.e: Nobody says it to you twice.

sn.s: Das ist eine Regel, die ich nicht erklären kann und die ich sicher weiss.
sn.e: That is a rule I cannot explain and that I know for certain.

sn.s: Wer es einmal gesagt hat, sagt es nie wieder.
sn.e: Whoever has said it once never says it again.

sn.s: Es wäre danach kein Satz mehr, sondern eine Gewohnheit.
sn.e: Afterwards it would no longer be a sentence, but a habit.

sn.s: Und eine Gewohnheit ist kein Lob.
sn.e: And a habit is not praise.

sn.s: Ich habe an dem Abend eine Liste im Kopf gemacht.
sn.e: That evening I made a list in my head.

sn.s: Was habe ich in drei Jahren gelernt, das man hören kann.
sn.e: What have I learnt in three years that you can hear.

sn.s: Ich sage merci und nicht danke.
sn.e: I say merci and not danke.

sn.s: Ich weiss, welcher Hügel welcher ist, wenn ich aus dem Zug schaue.
sn.e: I know which hill is which when I look out of the train.

sn.s: Ich sage Velo und Billett und Trottoir, ohne zu überlegen.
sn.e: I say Velo and Billett and Trottoir, without thinking.

sn.s: Ich sage halt und eben und mal, ohne sie zu planen.
sn.e: I say halt and eben and mal, without planning them.

sn.s: Ich antworte mit doch, wenn jemand etwas Falsches sagt.
sn.e: I answer with doch when somebody says something wrong.

sn.s: Ich sage nicht schlecht, wenn ich sehr gut meine.
sn.e: I say not bad when I mean very good.

sn.s: Ich stehe fünf Minuten vor der Zeit unten.
sn.e: I am downstairs five minutes early.

sn.s: Ich beklage mich über vier Minuten und meine es.
sn.e: I complain about four minutes and mean it.

sn.s: Ich sage nein ohne einen Grund und der Himmel fällt nicht.
sn.e: I say no without a reason and the sky does not fall.

sn.s: Ich frage nicht zuerst, wenn jemand etwas erzählen will.
sn.e: I do not ask first when somebody wants to tell something.

sn.s: Ich warte.
sn.e: I wait.

sn.s: Das Letzte ist das, was am längsten gedauert hat.
sn.e: The last one is the one that took the longest.

sn.s: Es steht in keinem Buch und niemand kann es einem sagen.
sn.e: It is in no book and nobody can tell it to you.

sn.s: Rosmarie hat es mir vor drei Jahren gesagt und ich habe es nicht verstanden.
sn.e: Rosmarie told me three years ago and I did not understand it.

sn.s: Sie ist gestorben, bevor ich es verstanden habe, und das ist meistens so.
sn.e: She died before I understood it, and that is mostly how it goes.

sn.s: Sie hat gesagt: Sie fragen nicht. Sie warten auf dich.
sn.e: She said: they do not ask. They wait for you.

sn.s: Ich habe zwei Jahre gebraucht, um zu merken, dass das umgekehrt auch gilt.
sn.e: It took me two years to notice that the reverse is also true.

sn.s: Es gibt eine Sache, die nicht auf der Liste steht.
sn.e: There is one thing that is not on the list.

sn.s: Ich träume immer noch nicht auf Deutsch.
sn.e: I still do not dream in German.

sn.s: Ich rechne immer noch nicht auf Deutsch.
sn.e: I still do not do arithmetic in German.

sn.s: Wenn ich mich schneide, fluche ich in meiner eigenen Sprache.
sn.e: When I cut myself, I swear in my own language.

sn.s: Ich glaube nicht, dass sich das ändert, und es stört mich nicht mehr.
sn.e: I do not think that changes, and it does not bother me any more.

sn.s: Am Abend habe ich es Selina erzählt.
sn.e: In the evening I told Selina about it.

sn.s: Sie hat gefragt: Und, was hast du gesagt?
sn.e: She asked: and, what did you say?

sn.s: Ich habe gesagt: Ich habe gesagt, dass es von ihm mehr zählt.
sn.e: I said: I said that it counts for more from him.

sn.s: Sie hat gesagt: Gut.
sn.e: She said: good.

sn.s: Dann hat sie gesagt: Und was hättest du vor zwei Jahren gesagt?
sn.e: Then she said: and what would you have said two years ago?

sn.s: Ich habe überlegt.
sn.e: I thought about it.

sn.s: Vor zwei Jahren hätte ich danke gesagt und dann drei Sätze zu viel.
sn.e: Two years ago I would have said thank you and then three sentences too many.

sn.s: Ich habe gesagt: Danke, aber mein Deutsch ist wirklich noch schlecht.
sn.e: I said: thank you, but my German is really still bad.

sn.s: Sie hat gelacht und gesagt: Eben.
sn.e: She laughed and said: eben.

sn.s: Und dann hat sie nichts mehr dazu gesagt.
sn.e: And then she said nothing more about it.

scenarios.title: Grüezi
scenarios.desc: Four people, and not one of them can be passed in silence
scenarios.setting: Your first morning. The lift, the pavement and the bakery, all before eight.

options.feedback: He said mitenand because there are three of you in the lift. You give it straight back, and that is the whole exchange.
Correct and nobody minds. Mitenand would have matched him exactly.
Eight floors of somebody knowing you did not answer. Nobody will mention it.
One word each and you both walk on. That is exactly what it is for.
Warm, and more than a stranger on a pavement was asking for. She will answer you.
Hoi is for people you know. To a stranger it lands as too familiar rather than friendly.
Greeting first, then what you want. That order is not optional here.
She greeted you and you went straight to the order. It is not rude, it is just a bit bare.

options.es: Ich möchte ein Brot und ein Gipfeli und zwei Weggli und Käse.
options.en: I would like a loaf and a Gipfeli and two Weggli and cheese.
options.feedback: No Grüezi at all, and all of it at once. Greet, then order, then add.
You take the leaving word she offered and hand it back. Two syllables and you are out of the door correctly.
Both correct German and both a little German German. Merci and Ade are what you hear in Luzern.
You will hear it, mostly from younger people, and to a woman behind a counter in Luzern it is the wrong register.

scenarios.title: Am Automaten
scenarios.desc: A ticket, a track and eight minutes
scenarios.setting: Zurich airport, underground, with a suitcase and no idea where track seven is.

steps.speaker: Der Automat
steps.en: Where would you like to travel to?

options.feedback: Nach for a town or a country. Short is right, it is a machine.
It works. Nach Luzern is the whole answer.
Zu goes to people and to buildings. Towns and countries take nach.

options.en: Yes, I am finished. Go ahead.
options.feedback: Bitte on its own is the whole of "go ahead". It does a great deal of work in this language.
Honest and fine if you are not. He will wait.
True, possibly, but bare. Einen Moment costs you nothing.

steps.speaker: Eine Frau am Perron
steps.en: Grüezi. Are you looking for something?

options.es: Ja, wo ist Gleis sieben, bitte?
options.en: Yes, where is track seven, please?
options.feedback: Gleis is the numbered track. She will point, or she will walk you there.

options.es: Wo ist der Zug nach Luzern?
options.en: Where is the train to Luzern?
options.feedback: She will understand and answer with a track number, which is what you needed anyway.
Bahnsteig is the German German word. Here it is the Perron, and the number on the board is the Gleis.

steps.speaker: Die Frau am Perron
steps.es: Dort unten, dann rechts. Sie haben noch vier Minuten.
steps.en: Down there, then right. You have four minutes left.

options.feedback: She gave you directions and a warning. Merci vielmal is the right size of thank you for both.
Fine. She did rather more than a plain merci.

options.es: Vier Minuten? Das ist zu wenig!
options.en: Four minutes? That is not enough!
options.feedback: Here four minutes is four minutes. She has told you it is enough by telling you the number.

scenarios.title: Ein Crème, bitte
scenarios.desc: Ordering the coffee, and the word for it
scenarios.setting: The café on the square. Lea is behind the counter and it is not busy.

steps.speaker: Lea
steps.en: Grüezi. What can I get you?

options.feedback: Exactly what you said on your first day, and it works. She will ask you which kind.
The Swiss standard coffee, ordered by its name. This is what you learn on day two.
No greeting and no bitte. She will still bring it and she will still notice.
You did not know the second word and you picked the one you did know. That is the right move every time.
Asking is not a failure. She will tell you, and you will own the word by tomorrow.
She asked which, not whether. You will get whichever she guesses.

steps.speaker: Lea
steps.en: Would you like something to eat as well?

options.feedback: Nein merci is softer than nein on its own, and it is what people actually say.
Coffee and a Gipfeli is the whole Swiss breakfast and nobody will find it odd at three in the afternoon either.
Understood, and a little flat. Merci does the softening.

options.en: (put down four fifty) There you go.
options.feedback: The exact money, so she does not have to give you anything back. Bitte covers the handing over.

options.en: (hand over a twenty) There you go.
options.feedback: Perfectly normal. She will count your change out loud.

options.en: (hand over a two hundred) There you go.
options.feedback: For a four-franc coffee. She will take it, and she will look at you first.

scenarios.title: In der Bäckerei
scenarios.desc: Pointing at things until you have their names
scenarios.setting: Half past six in the morning. Everything is out and nothing is labelled.

options.es: Grüezi. (auf etwas zeigen) Was ist das, bitte?
options.en: Grüezi. (point at something) What is that, please?
options.feedback: Pointing is not cheating. It is how you get the word, and you only need it once per thing.
You know the word already. No article needed with a number.
She will hand it over. A Grüezi in front of it costs one syllable.

steps.speaker: Die Verkäuferin
steps.es: Das ist ein Gipfeli. Möchten Sie eines?
steps.en: That is a Gipfeli. Would you like one?

options.feedback: You take the word she just gave you and use it in the same breath. That is how it sticks.
Also right, and now you have one for the walk and one for later.
She will know exactly what you mean. She has just told you what it is called here, and you used the other word anyway.
She asked an open question and you answered it. This is the point where you add the thing you nearly forgot.
Das ist alles closes the order cleanly.
Fine, if a little short. Nein merci is what she said to you.
Fine, and it costs a few Rappen. Most people here have one in their pocket already.
The answer of somebody who has been here more than a week.
Tüte is the German German word. In Switzerland it is a Sack, and it is not free.

scenarios.title: An der Kasse
scenarios.desc: Paying, and getting a look
scenarios.setting: The Migros till on a Friday. Three people behind you and it moves fast.

steps.speaker: Die Frau an der Kasse
steps.en: Grüezi. Do you have a Cumulus card?

options.feedback: You have no idea what it is and it does not matter. Nein merci is a complete answer.
A fair question with nobody behind you. On a Friday evening she will answer it fast.
She will wait for you to produce it, and you do not have one.

options.en: (hand over thirty francs) There you go.
options.feedback: Five Rappen back and everybody moves on. This is what the .95 is for.
Nobody will sigh at you. They will all watch, though.
Perfectly normal if you did not catch it. She will say the number again, slower.

steps.speaker: Die Frau an der Kasse
steps.es: Fünf Rappen zurück. Möchten Sie den Bon?
steps.en: Five Rappen back. Would you like the receipt?

options.feedback: Two words and you are done. She is already scanning the next person.
Nothing wrong with it at all.
It is nothing, and it is also her till balancing at the end of the day.

steps.speaker: Die Frau an der Kasse
steps.en: Thanks very much. Have a good evening.

options.feedback: Gleichfalls is the one word that gives a good-wish straight back, and it works for every one of them.
Completely fine and what most people say.
She wished you something. Two syllables would have covered it.

scenarios.title: Wo ist die Post?
scenarios.desc: Asking, and understanding half the answer
scenarios.setting: You have been walking in circles for ten minutes and every street looks the same.

options.es: Grüezi. Entschuldigung, wo ist die Post?
options.en: Grüezi. Excuse me, where is the post office?
options.feedback: Greeting, apology, question. Three beats and you have not wasted a second of her time.

options.en: Grüezi. I am looking for the post office.
options.feedback: A statement rather than a question, and it works just as well.
She will help you anyway. One word thrown at a stranger is not how it is done here.

steps.speaker: Die Frau
steps.es: Da vorne links, dann geradeaus, und dann noch einmal rechts.
steps.en: Up ahead on the left, then straight on, and then right again.

options.feedback: Repeating it back is how you find out whether you got it, and it takes two seconds.
Asking again is not embarrassing. Walking twenty minutes the wrong way is.
You did not get it and you have just told her you did. You will be back here in five minutes.

steps.speaker: Die Frau
steps.es: Kommen Sie, ich gehe mit. Es ist nicht weit.
steps.en: Come on, I will come with you. It is not far.

options.es: Merci vielmal. Das ist sehr freundlich.
options.en: Thanks very much. That is very kind.
options.feedback: Accept it. This is the normal answer here and refusing makes it awkward for both of you.
She will let you go. She was not being polite, she genuinely finds it easier than explaining.

options.en: No. I will find it myself.
options.feedback: Flat, and she was doing you a kindness. Nein, nein, das geht schon does the same job without the edge.

steps.speaker: Die Frau
steps.es: So, das gelbe Haus dort. Das ist die Post.
steps.en: There, the yellow building there. That is the post office.

options.feedback: She walked five minutes out of her way. Merci vielmal, not merci.

options.es: Gelb. Das merke ich mir. Merci.
options.en: Yellow. I will remember that. Merci.
options.feedback: And you should. The post office is yellow in every town in the country.
A little thin for somebody who escorted you there.

scenarios.title: Am Brunnen
scenarios.desc: The water is free and somebody will tell you
scenarios.setting: A hot afternoon on the square, with a two-franc bottle of water in your hand.

options.feedback: She is going somewhere with this. Answer and let her get there.

options.es: Grüezi. Ja, es ist warm heute.
options.en: Grüezi. Yes, it is warm today.
options.feedback: The weather, offered back. That is how a conversation starts here.
She greeted you first. One word back leaves the greeting hanging.

steps.speaker: Die alte Frau
steps.es: Sie müssen das Wasser nicht kaufen. Dort ist ein Brunnen.
steps.en: You do not have to buy water. There is a fountain over there.

options.feedback: The obvious question, and asking it is how you stop buying water for good.
She has just saved you two francs a day. Take it.

options.es: Das Wasser im Brunnen? Nein, merci.
options.en: The water in the fountain? No, thanks.
options.feedback: She is not offering you puddle water. Almost every fountain in the country runs drinking water.

steps.speaker: Die alte Frau
steps.es: Natürlich. Fast alle Brunnen sind Trinkwasser.
steps.en: Of course. Almost all the fountains are drinking water.

options.feedback: Exactly the right follow-up. There is a sign, and it says kein Trinkwasser.
Go and fill the bottle you already paid for. That is the whole trick.

options.es: In der Stadt? Das ist nicht sauber.
options.en: In town? That is not clean.
options.feedback: It comes off the mountain and it is colder and cleaner than the bottle in your hand.

steps.speaker: Die alte Frau
steps.es: Das macht jeder am Anfang. Ade.
steps.en: Everybody does that at the start. Goodbye.

options.feedback: She told you something useful and did not make you feel stupid. That deserves the full merci vielmal.
Correct, and it skips the thank you she had earned.

options.en: I am not at the start.
options.feedback: You are, and she was being kind about it.

scenarios.title: Am Samstagabend
scenarios.desc: The shop shut two hours ago
scenarios.setting: Half past six on a Saturday, no milk in the flat, and everything dark.

steps.speaker: Ein Mann vor dem Laden
steps.es: Der ist schon zu. Seit fünf.
steps.en: It has been shut since five.

options.feedback: Say the thing you cannot believe. He will explain it, because everybody here has had this conversation.
Fine, and it ends the conversation before he tells you the useful part.

options.es: Aber es ist erst halb sieben.
options.en: But it is only half past six.
options.feedback: It is, and the shop shut at five regardless. Arguing with the opening hours is a beginner move.

steps.speaker: Der Mann
steps.es: Am Samstag schliessen die Läden früh. Und am Sonntag ist alles zu.
steps.en: On Saturday the shops close early. And on Sunday everything is shut.

options.feedback: Yes. This is the single most useful fact anybody will tell you in your first month.
Sometimes it opens for an hour or two in the morning. That is the whole exception, apart from the station.

options.es: Das ist nicht gut für den Laden.
options.en: That is not good for the shop.
options.feedback: Everybody here has decided otherwise, repeatedly, at the ballot box.

steps.speaker: Der Mann
steps.es: Am Bahnhof ist etwas offen. Auch am Sonntag.
steps.en: There is something open at the station. On Sunday too.

options.en: At the station? Thanks very much!
options.feedback: The station shops are the exception the whole country runs on. Now you know it too.
Yes. And it is open, which on a Sunday is the only thing that matters.
It is a fifteen minute walk and the alternative is no milk until Monday.

steps.speaker: Der Mann
steps.es: Nächstes Mal am Freitag einkaufen. Ade.
steps.en: Do your shopping on Friday next time. Goodbye.

options.en: Thanks. I will do that. Goodbye.
options.feedback: You will, and by the third weekend it will not be a decision any more.
He gave you the rule and the exception in under a minute. Worth the vielmal.
He stopped in the street to save you a wasted Sunday.

scenarios.title: Die Schlüsselübergabe
scenarios.desc: Three keys and a great deal of information
scenarios.setting: Two o’clock, an empty flat, and a landlord who says everything twice.

steps.speaker: Herr Kaufmann
steps.es: Grüezi. Also, das ist die Wohnung.
steps.en: Grüezi. So, this is the flat.

options.feedback: His name back to him. Nobody here minds being called by it, and using it says you were listening.
Fine. Merci is the word you will hear back from him.
It is empty because it was handed over cleaned to the corner, which is what he is about to explain.

steps.speaker: Herr Kaufmann
steps.es: Der erste Schlüssel ist für die Wohnung, der zweite für das Haus.
steps.en: The first key is for the flat, the second for the building.

options.feedback: There is always a third and it is always the cellar. Asking is quicker than being told twice.
He will say it again anyway. He says everything twice.
You do. The cellar is where your bike is going to live.

steps.speaker: Herr Kaufmann
steps.es: Nach dem Duschen müssen Sie das Fenster aufmachen. Sonst gibt es Schimmel.
steps.en: After showering you have to open the window. Otherwise you get mould.

options.feedback: Short and it is a promise. Mould at the handover comes out of your deposit.
Especially in winter. Asking shows you took it as a rule and not as small talk.
He will let that pass and he will remember it.

steps.speaker: Herr Kaufmann
steps.es: Die Miete müssen Sie bis am dritten bezahlen. Nicht am vierten.
steps.en: You have to pay the rent by the third. Not the fourth.

options.es: Bis am dritten. Ich schreibe es auf.
options.en: By the third. I will write it down.
options.feedback: He said a date and a not-date. Repeating the date back is the whole answer.
True, and it does not show him you registered which day.
Then a Mahnung comes, it costs twenty francs, and you have just told your landlord you might.

scenarios.title: Am Dienstag gewaschen
scenarios.desc: You used the machine on somebody else’s day
scenarios.setting: The laundry room, two hours later, with your washing still in the machine.

steps.speaker: Frau Steiner
steps.es: Entschuldigung. Der Dienstag ist mein Tag.
steps.en: Excuse me. Tuesday is my day.

options.feedback: She is right, and saying so ends it. Nobody here wants an argument, they want the rota kept.

options.es: Die Maschine ist leer. Ich dachte, es geht.
options.en: The machine was empty. I thought it was fine.
options.feedback: A reason, which she will accept and not agree with. Empty is not the same as free.

options.en: But nobody is using it right now.
options.feedback: That is the argument, and it is the one that makes an enemy in a building you will live in for years.

steps.speaker: Frau Steiner
steps.es: Sie müssen sich in den Plan eintragen. Dann gehört der Tag Ihnen.
steps.en: You have to sign into the rota. Then the day is yours.

options.es: Ich trage mich das nächste Mal ein.
options.en: I will sign myself in next time.
options.feedback: Uses her own verb back. eintragen is the word the whole system runs on.
On the wall by the door. Asking is better than guessing again.
Yes, and it is in the Hausordnung, which she knows and now knows you have not read.

steps.speaker: Frau Steiner
steps.es: Nehmen Sie Ihre Wäsche heraus. Ich brauche die Maschine jetzt.
steps.en: Take your washing out. I need the machine now.

options.feedback: Immediate and one more apology. That closes it properly.
The Tumbler is Tuesday’s too. You are asking for the second half of the day you already took.
Reasonable, and she has been waiting two hours already.

steps.speaker: Frau Amrein
steps.es: Und? War die Frau Steiner böse?

options.feedback: The right answer, and she will report it to the building exactly as you said it.
Honest. She will tell you Frau Steiner is never cross, which is nearly true.

options.en: How do you know about it already?
options.feedback: She always knows already. Asking her that is a joke she will enjoy.

scenarios.title: Beim Hauswart
scenarios.desc: Reporting a problem, in the one hour he is there
scenarios.setting: Five o’clock, the ground floor, and a bathroom light that stopped working yesterday.

options.es: Grüezi. Das Licht im Bad ist kaputt.
options.en: Grüezi. The bathroom light is broken.
options.feedback: Greeting and then the problem in one short sentence. He is waiting for exactly that and nothing else.

options.en: Grüezi. Do you have a moment?
options.feedback: Polite, and it makes him ask what for. He would rather you just said it.
Not unfriendly, just not what this hour is for. He will wait for the actual reason.
Two words. He is already writing it in the book.

options.en: The flat next to Frau Amrein.
options.feedback: He knows exactly which one that is. The number is faster.

options.es: Ich wohne seit einem Monat hier.
options.en: I have been living here a month.
options.feedback: Not the question. He asked which flat.
He will be there at eight. Not five past. Take the time and say thank you.
It could, and you have just made work out of something that was finished.

options.es: Können Sie es heute noch machen?
options.en: Could you still do it today?
options.feedback: You report a problem to him. You do not set his schedule.

options.en: Thanks very much. That was quick.
options.feedback: Four minutes. Noticing it out loud is the closest thing to a compliment he will accept.
Fine. He will nod and pack up.
He will tell you in about six words. It is a fair question.

scenarios.title: Bei der Gemeinde
scenarios.desc: Registering, in eleven minutes
scenarios.setting: Eight in the morning, ticket B twelve, and a folder with four documents in it.

steps.speaker: Der Beamte
steps.es: Grüezi. Was kann ich für Sie tun?
steps.en: Grüezi. What can I do for you?

options.en: Grüezi. I would like to register.
options.feedback: The exact sentence for the exact counter. He will have the form out before you finish it.
True, and he still has to ask what you want. anmelden is the word.

options.en: Grüezi. I need a bank account.
options.feedback: Wrong building. But you do need this first, and the bank will ask for what he is about to give you.
bitte handing something over is one of the four jobs that word does.
It is. Asking costs nothing.
Then this is a second trip. Bring everything, every time.

steps.speaker: Der Beamte
steps.es: Und die Religion? Sie müssen das nicht ausfüllen.
steps.en: And religion? You do not have to fill that in.

options.feedback: Because the church is funded by tax here. He will tell you plainly and it is worth knowing.

options.en: Then I will leave it empty.
options.feedback: He told you it was optional. Taking him at his word is fine.

options.en: Do I have to fill that in?
options.feedback: He has just said you do not. Worth listening to the second half of the sentence.

steps.speaker: Der Beamte
steps.es: So. Das ist die Bestätigung. Willkommen in Luzern.
steps.en: There. That is your confirmation. Welcome to Luzern.

options.feedback: He meant the welcome. It is said without ceremony and it is not nothing.
For the bank and for the insurer. Do not lose it, which is what he is about to say.
It is. Eleven minutes, which will keep surprising you.

scenarios.title: Der Nachbar an der Tür
scenarios.desc: He came up two floors in his socks
scenarios.setting: Three in the afternoon. You have just dragged a table across a wooden floor twice.

steps.speaker: Herr Bucher
steps.es: Grüezi. Ich bin Bucher, von unten.
steps.en: Grüezi. I am Bucher, from downstairs.

options.feedback: You know why he is here and you say so first. That is the whole conversation over in one line.

options.es: Grüezi. Was kann ich für Sie tun?
options.en: Grüezi. What can I do for you?
options.feedback: Polite, and it makes him say the awkward part out loud.

options.es: Grüezi. Es ist erst drei Uhr.
options.en: Grüezi. It is only three o’clock.
options.feedback: It is, and he works at home, which he has not told you yet because you did not let him.

options.en: I did not know that. Sorry.
options.feedback: He is not complaining, he is telling you a fact you needed. Take it that way.

options.en: I will not move anything else.
options.feedback: Concrete, and it is the thing he actually wants.
Yes. And now you know why the building is silent at eleven in the morning.

options.es: Nein. Aber ich kann einen kaufen.
options.en: No. But I can buy one.
options.feedback: That is the answer he came up two floors for, and he did not have to ask for it.
It does, a lot, and asking makes it his suggestion rather than your concession.
He would not have mentioned it otherwise.

options.es: Grüezi, Herr Bucher. Gut, merci. Und Ihnen?
options.en: Grüezi, Herr Bucher. Good, thanks. And you?
options.feedback: Two weeks and a rug later, he is asking. That is not a small thing here — answer it properly and ask back.
Correct and it leaves his question half answered. The Und Ihnen is the other half.
The everyday answer, and it lands as easy rather than formal. He will use it back at you.

scenarios.title: Bei Nuno
scenarios.desc: Friday at seven, and he does come at seven
scenarios.setting: A kitchen after service, a bottle of something, and the first person here who talks fast.

options.feedback: Hoi back, not Grüezi. He offered du and the informal greeting in one word, and taking it is the answer.
Not wrong, and it is a step more formal than what he just gave you. He will not mind and he will notice.
The other informal one. Same register, and it is what you would hear around Zurich and the centre.

steps.speaker: Nuno
steps.es: Und? Wie ist der erste Monat?
steps.en: Well? How is the first month?

options.feedback: Two words and he will laugh, because it is exactly right and he remembers it.
Honest, and it opens the conversation he wants to have.
True, and it is the thing every newcomer says first. He has heard it eighteen years running.

steps.speaker: Nuno
steps.es: Lern die Artikel jetzt. Sofort. Nicht später.
steps.en: Learn the articles now. Straight away. Not later.

options.es: Der Tisch, die Wohnung, das Bad.
options.en: Der Tisch, die Wohnung, das Bad.
options.feedback: You did not agree, you demonstrated. That is the only answer he wanted.
They do. And everybody hears it, which is what he is trying to tell you.
This is the one piece of advice he gives everybody, because nobody gave it to him.

steps.speaker: Nuno
steps.es: Die Fehler sind nicht das Problem. Das Schweigen ist das Problem.
steps.en: The mistakes are not the problem. The silence is the problem.

options.feedback: You do. Forty minutes at an airport without saying a word taught you the same thing.

options.es: Zwei Jahre still. Das ist lang.
options.en: Two years silent. That is a long time.
options.feedback: It is, and he said it about himself. Repeating it back shows you heard which part mattered.

options.es: Ich habe keine Angst vor Fehlern.
options.en: I am not afraid of mistakes.
options.feedback: Everybody says that in the first month. He will simply keep talking to you and find out.

scenarios.title: Das Übliche?
scenarios.desc: Somebody starts your coffee before you get there
scenarios.setting: Quarter past seven, the machine already running, and a question that is not really a question.

options.feedback: Two words, and the second one carries all of it. Gern is how enthusiasm is said here.
You gave her the word back. That is exactly what a regular does with it.
Fair, the first time. But she has watched you order the same thing forty mornings running.
Three words and it is true. She has heard it from everybody who arrives, and she asks anyway.
Correct and closed. One sentence more is what turns this into a conversation.
A closed door. Ja on its own ends it, and she was opening something.
You do. And agreeing with a small direct observation is the whole answer here.

options.en: I do not have much time.
options.feedback: True, and she will point out that the coffee costs the same sitting down.
She has watched you do it for a month. This is a correction and it is meant kindly.
You said it back. Ade is for a guest, bis morgen is for somebody who is coming back.
Not wrong, and it is the more distant of the two. She just gave you the closer one.
You will be there at quarter past seven and both of you know it.

scenarios.title: Vier Minuten
scenarios.desc: The bus is late and somebody looks at the sky
scenarios.setting: A bus stop, rain on the shelter, and a woman with a very old dog.

options.es: Ja. Gestern hat es den ganzen Tag geregnet.
options.en: Yes. Yesterday it rained all day.
options.feedback: Yes plus one sentence. The weather is the door, and you walked through it.
Polite and finished. She will not push, and nothing more will happen.
She knows. She was not making a claim about the weather, she was asking whether you want to talk.
A small failure of your own, offered up. It is the fastest way past the weather.
True and short. She has one too, and she left it on the bus.
Not a mistake. But every no here can carry a second sentence and this one does not.
Seit takes the dative, and this is the answer everybody gives. You will say it a hundred times.
Seit einem. The dative is not optional here and it is the commonest slip in the first year.
Fine. Her next question was going to be how long, so you can save her the trouble.

options.en: I like the town very much.
options.feedback: Gefallen puts the thing in charge: it pleases me. The person goes in the dative and stays there.
Backwards, and it says something else entirely. The town does the pleasing, not you.
Warm enough. Name the thing you like and she will tell you where to sit in spring.

scenarios.title: Woher kommst du?
scenarios.desc: The question you will answer a thousand times
scenarios.setting: An apéro, a glass in your hand, and a man who has asked this before.

options.es: Aus dem Süden. Aus einer kleinen Stadt.
options.en: From the south. From a small town.
options.feedback: The place, then the country. Here the part matters more than the nation, and he will ask which part anyway.
No edge is meant. He asks a man from Bern the same thing and hears it in the vowels.
Charming and it dodges. He will simply ask again, more slowly.

steps.speaker: Marco
steps.es: Und seit wann sind Sie hier?
steps.en: And since when have you been here?

options.feedback: Seit einem Monat, seit einer Woche, seit einem Jahr. Nuno still gets asked after eighteen years.
Understood, and it drops the word that carries the sense. Seit is what makes it a stretch of time.
That is the day you arrived. Seit is the whole month since, and he asked for the month.

options.es: Ich arbeite in einem Büro. Zahlen und Briefe.
options.en: I work in an office. Numbers and letters.
options.feedback: Plain, and plain is the register. Nobody will ask what you earn, and nobody thinks less of the answer.
He asked what you trained as, which here usually means an apprenticeship. Two of three people did one.
Money does not come into this conversation. It will not come into any of them.

steps.speaker: Marco
steps.es: Mein Bruder wohnt auch im Süden.
steps.en: My brother lives in the south too.

options.feedback: You asked back. He has been waiting for somebody to, and now you will hear about the brother.
He opened a door with his own family in it. One question is all it needed.
He gave you something personal. Ja hands it straight back unopened.

scenarios.title: Zum Wohl
scenarios.desc: Eight people, eight glasses, and one rule
scenarios.setting: Half past five, everybody standing, and a plate of olives nobody is eating from.

steps.speaker: Petra
steps.en: Would you like a glass of wine?

options.feedback: Gern does the work, and naming what you want saves a second question.

options.en: No, thank you. A water, please.
options.feedback: Nobody asks twice and nobody minds. A water is a glass, and a glass is all this needs.
She will pour you something. But the offer was a small question with a small answer.
The name, and her eyes, and only then the glass. All three or it does not count.
Half of it. The name is not decoration here, it is the part people notice is missing.
Heard here too, and it is the louder one. Zum Wohl is what an apéro in Luzern mostly says, and it is what she just said.

options.es: Nein. Ich habe gedacht, es gibt Abendessen.
options.en: No. I thought there would be dinner.
options.feedback: Every newcomer makes this mistake once. An apéro is a glass and four olives, and it ends at seven.
Then somebody told you, or you learned it the hard way. Either way you are ahead.
Three olives and four nuts. Not half the plate, which is what hunger does to a newcomer.
It is seven, and at seven everybody puts the glass down at the same moment with no signal at all.
It is early. It is also over, and that is the shape of the thing rather than a judgement on it.
An apéro has an end time the way it has a start time. Asking her to stay puts her in an awkward spot.

scenarios.title: Wollen wir du sagen?
scenarios.desc: A cake, a first name, and a small ceremony
scenarios.setting: Sunday afternoon, your own doorway, and the woman who has said Sie for five weeks.

options.feedback: And then your own first name back. That is the whole ceremony: two first names and a handshake.
You missed it. She gave you her first name after five weeks of not giving it.
You knew the name. She was not telling you the name, she was offering you the du.
The offer comes from the older person and it comes once. Yes is very nearly the only answer.
Still on Sie in the sentence that agrees to leave it. She will laugh, and she will not mind.
Possible, and it is a real refusal of something she thought about for five weeks first.
Dir, not Ihnen. The mouth takes about three weeks to catch up and she has already said so.
The slip everybody makes. She will just say her first name again and wait.
Honest and small, which is the register. Es geht is a real answer here and not a complaint.
Du and the first name in one sentence. That is the pairing, and it is the part that takes practice.
Du and Frau Amrein do not go together. Pick one register and this one is already picked.

options.es: Nein, danke. Ich mache uns einen.
options.en: No, thank you. I will make us one.
options.feedback: Better than accepting. She came across the landing with a cake and you can cross it back.

scenarios.title: Am Tisch
scenarios.desc: Three hours, one small pan, and no hurry at all
scenarios.setting: A flat the same shape as yours, forty years older, and an oven in the middle of the table.

options.feedback: Short is right. This is the first time you have been past her door and neither of you will mention that.
There are two chairs. One of them is hers and has been for forty years.
Setz dich is an instruction shaped like an offer. Raclette is a table you sit at.
Gib mir: the person in the dative, the thing in the accusative. It is the shape of half this evening.

options.en: I am giving you the cheese.
options.feedback: Dir and den. Both cases in one short sentence, and you built it right.
Dir. The person receiving always sits in the dative, with geben, zeigen, schicken and schenken alike.
Fein is for food. Gut is for work and for weather, and using it here marks you out at once.
Understood, and it is the word for a job well done rather than for a plate.
She has made this for you for three hours. Es geht is what you say about a bus.

steps.speaker: Rosmarie
steps.en: Do not drink anything cold with it.

options.en: Then I will have a tea.
options.feedback: Tea or white wine. Whether the rule is true is beside the point: her mother said it.
You will get the explanation, and the explanation is that her mother said so. It is enough.
It may not be. It is also her table, her cheese, and a thing she has believed for seventy years.

scenarios.title: Am Samstag?
scenarios.desc: An invitation with a date in it, and one without
scenarios.setting: After the club, a car park, and somebody deciding how much to commit to.

steps.speaker: Timo
steps.en: We should eat together some time.

options.es: Gern. Hast du am Freitag Zeit?
options.en: Gladly. Are you free on Friday?
options.feedback: You turned mal into a date. That is the whole move, and it is the one nobody expects you to make.
Warm and it commits nobody. Mal has no date in it, so nothing will happen unless somebody adds one.
Fair question, and a slightly hard one. Naming a day yourself is easier for both of you.

steps.speaker: Timo
steps.es: Freitag geht nicht. Der Dienstag danach?
steps.en: Friday does not work. The Tuesday after?

options.feedback: Settled, and nobody will mention it again until Tuesday. That is what an arrangement is here.
Maybe is not an answer to a date. Say yes or say no and either one is fine.

options.es: Ich schaue noch. Ich sage dir Bescheid.
options.en: I will see. I will let you know.
options.feedback: Honest, and it puts the work on him. He got his calendar out of his bag for this.

steps.speaker: Timo
steps.es: Kommst du am Samstag ans Spiel?
steps.en: Are you coming to the match on Saturday?

options.es: Ja, gern. Um wie viel Uhr?
options.feedback: Yes and then the practical question. Both halves, in that order.

options.es: Ich habe leider schon etwas abgemacht.
options.en: Unfortunately I have already arranged something.
options.feedback: Leider, and no reason. Nobody asks what, and the reason stays yours.
It is Wednesday. By local arithmetic three days out is practically the day itself.

steps.speaker: Timo
steps.es: Also am Dienstag um halb acht.
steps.en: So Tuesday at half past seven.

options.es: Ich bin um zwanzig nach da.
options.en: I will be there at twenty past.
options.feedback: Five minutes early is on time. Saying so out loud is not fussy here, it is normal.
Done. He will be outside at twenty-five past and so, now, will you.
Half past seven is half past seven. Roughly is what the message four minutes beforehand is for.

scenarios.title: In der Gruppe
scenarios.desc: Fourteen people, eighty messages, and one thumb
scenarios.setting: Your phone on the table at nine in the evening, going off every forty seconds.

steps.speaker: Timo
steps.es: Samstag Grillieren bei mir. Wer kommt?
steps.en: Barbecue at my place on Saturday. Who is coming?

options.en: I will be there. At seven?
options.feedback: Short, and it drops the ich. That is the register for messages and a long sentence reads as a problem.

options.es: Ich komme sehr gern und freue mich schon.
options.en: I am coming very gladly and am already looking forward to it.
options.feedback: Nothing is wrong with it. It is four times longer than every other reply and he will ask if you are all right.
A thumb is a yes. Not I have read this: I am coming. People have been counted absent for the difference.
Two words and it is binding. Nobody will ask again, and the bread had better be there.
Now nobody knows whether there is bread. In a group of fourteen, maybe is worse than no.
Fine. Ask in the group rather than to him alone, and somebody will name a thing.
He is seventy-one, he sends the same picture of flowers every morning at six, and nobody answers. Nobody minds either.
Kind, and now there are two messages where the group expected none. He will be pleased.

options.en: It is six in the morning.
options.feedback: It is. He has been up since half past four and this is what he does with the hour.

steps.speaker: Timo
steps.es: Du warst nicht da. Alles gut?
steps.en: You were not there. Everything all right?

options.es: Es tut mir leid. Ich habe nur den Daumen geschickt.
options.en: I am sorry. I only sent the thumb.
options.feedback: Said on the same day it is nothing. Left for three days it becomes a thing, and Nuno will tell you so.
You sent a thumb. Here that is the yes, and the argument will not go your way.
Fine as far as it goes. Sending that on Friday instead of explaining it on Wednesday is the fix.

scenarios.title: Der Anschluss ist weg
scenarios.desc: Forty seconds, and eight people who do not mind
scenarios.setting: A platform in Hergiswil, the other train pulling out, and a loudspeaker about to apologise.

options.en: Here you are. And the Halbtax.
options.feedback: Both together. A Halbtax price with no card is not a valid ticket, and that costs a hundred francs.
He will ask for the card next. Handing over both saves the second question.

options.es: Ich habe es am Automaten gekauft.
options.en: I bought it at the machine.
options.feedback: He did not ask where it came from. He asked to see it.

options.en: Yes. When does the next one go?
options.feedback: The practical question, and he will have the answer before the loudspeaker does.
Nobody said it was. Eight other people on that platform missed it too and none of them said a word.

options.en: How long do I have to wait?
options.feedback: Also fine, and it is the same question from the other end.
Short. He has forty more people to get through and he says thank you to every one of them.
It is not. And the announcement is about to apologise for it, which is somehow worse.
Fair. It is usually the platform you are standing on, which is not an accident.

options.en: I will be twenty minutes late.
options.feedback: Four words and the problem is gone. Twenty minutes with a message is nothing; twenty without is a thing.

options.es: Anschluss verpasst. Bin um halb da.
options.en: Missed my connection. I will be there at half past.
options.feedback: Even better. He knows the line and the word Anschluss explains all of it.

options.es: Der Zug hatte Verspätung und dann war der andere Zug schon weg.
options.en: The train was delayed and then the other train had already gone.
options.feedback: All true and four times longer than it needs to be. A long message reads as a big problem.

scenarios.title: Auf dem Schiff
scenarios.desc: The bus on the water, and it is faster
scenarios.setting: A landing stage behind the station, thirty people, half of them with rucksacks.

options.feedback: Say the card at the same time. She is about to ask, and half the queue behind you has one.
Fine. Then comes: mit Halbtax? and then the price twice over.
The boat goes in six minutes. Buy the return, it costs less than two singles.

steps.speaker: Frau am Schalter
steps.es: Gilt auch für den Bus zurück.
steps.en: It is valid for the bus back too.

options.feedback: One ticket from A to B, and whatever runs in between is your business. Train, bus, boat, the same card.

options.en: Do I have to buy anything else?
options.feedback: No. That is exactly what she just told you.
Good question, and the answer is usually no. Mountain railways are their own thing, and the Halbtax still halves them.

steps.speaker: Mann an Bord
steps.en: Are you sitting up top or below?

options.es: Oben. Ich bin noch nicht so lange hier.
options.en: Up top. I have not been here that long.
options.feedback: Honest, and he will laugh. Tourists sit up top; everybody else sits below with the newspaper.
The local answer. It is thirty-five minutes and you have seen the lake before.
It is not. He was making conversation, which is the whole thing that happens on a boat.

options.es: Und es fährt noch jeden Tag?
options.en: And it still runs every day?
options.feedback: It does, in the timetable, with tickets. That is the part worth being surprised by, and he will tell you all of it.
He opened a door. One question and you get twenty minutes about the engine.
It does. That is a steam engine and there is a man standing next to it whose whole job is watching it.

scenarios.title: Auf dem Gipfel
scenarios.desc: Everybody says du up here, and nobody does down there
scenarios.setting: Two thousand metres, twenty people, and a white blanket over the whole lake below.

options.feedback: Hoi back, and du, because you are on a mountain. Down in the town this would be Grüezi and Sie.
Not wrong and a step more formal than what she just gave you. Up here that reads as a little stiff.
On a summit, with a rucksack, at eleven in the morning. Nobody says that here.

steps.speaker: Selina
steps.en: Did you come up on foot?

options.feedback: True, and there is no shame in it. She walked four hours and will not say a word about the difference.
Better still. It answers and it says something about you at the same time.
Your shoes say otherwise. She looked at them before she asked.

steps.speaker: Selina
steps.es: Ich bin um halb sechs losgegangen.
steps.en: I set off at half past five.

options.feedback: Ask back. She got out of the fog into the sun at about seven and she would like somebody to hear it.
Fair reaction. It is also completely normal here, and she will say so.

options.es: Das ist zu früh für mich.
options.en: That is too early for me.
options.feedback: Honest, and it turns her morning into a fact about you.
The true answer, and she will nod and not ask again. Nobody else has asked you this at all.
Bigger than you know. She asked the one question everybody here avoids, so she will hear the size of it.
Because she wanted to know. It is the first real question anybody has put to you in nine months.

scenarios.title: Am falschen Weg
scenarios.desc: Lost, marked, and mildly embarrassed
scenarios.setting: A meadow with no path in it, no signal, and a dog barking somewhere below.

options.es: Grüezi. Entschuldigung, können Sie mir helfen?
options.en: Hello. Excuse me, can you help me?
options.feedback: Greet first, then ask. Können Sie mir is the polite opening and it costs you two words.
No greeting and no können Sie. It is understood and it lands like an instruction.
Grüezi, not hallo. And you do not have a problem, you have a wrong turning.

steps.speaker: Frau mit Hunden
steps.en: Where do you want to get to?

options.feedback: Sich verlaufen, and the sich is not optional. Saying it plainly is faster than explaining the route.
Ich habe mich verlaufen. Without the sich it is not a sentence anybody says.

options.es: Zur Hütte. Aber ich finde den Weg nicht.
options.en: To the hut. But I cannot find the path.
options.feedback: Answers her question and states the problem. She asked where to, so tell her where to.

steps.speaker: Frau mit Hunden
steps.es: Ah. Sie sind zu weit links.
steps.en: Ah. You are too far to the left.

options.feedback: The useful question. Twenty minutes, and she is about to offer to walk them with you.
She will wave it away. A lot of people do it there, which is exactly what she says next.
The sign was not wrong. There were three paths and two names and you picked on looks.

steps.speaker: Frau mit Hunden
steps.es: Ich gehe auch dorthin. Kommen Sie.
steps.en: I am going there too. Come along.

options.feedback: She is not going there. You will work that out twenty minutes later, at the sign, when she turns round.
You will not, and refusing help on a mountain is the one place where politeness is the wrong instinct.
Fine, and it is more words than the moment needs. She already decided.

scenarios.title: Der letzte Zug
scenarios.desc: Everybody at the table knows their own
scenarios.setting: Quarter past midnight in a pub, one story unfinished, and four different departure times.

options.feedback: Let him go. He said it in the middle of a sentence because that is how you catch a train without running.
His train is at twelve thirty-two and there is not another one. Asking is putting him in a corner.

options.es: Und der Rest von der Geschichte?
options.en: And the rest of the story?
options.feedback: You will get it next time. Everybody here has an unfinished story with somebody.

steps.speaker: Marco
steps.en: And you? When does yours go?

options.es: Zwanzig nach. Ich habe noch Zeit.
options.en: Twenty past. I still have time.
options.feedback: Everybody has a number and everybody says it without checking. Yours is the twenty past bus.
Then you will be running at eighteen past, and running is the part people notice.
Eighty francs to Stans, less from here. Nobody does it, and saying so makes the table go quiet.
That is how it works and it is not meanness. Paying for somebody else needs a reason.
He will ask why, and he will really be asking. There is nothing wrong with it and it needs a reason.
There is no later. Pay at quarter past and you leave at ten past without a jacket in one hand.
Say it to each person, by name if you can. It takes thirty seconds and it is why you leave at ten past.
Understood everywhere and it is the German one. Ade is what this table says.

options.en: See you tomorrow at the office.
options.feedback: Warm, specific, and it names the next time. That is the whole move.

scenarios.title: Rigi oder Pilatus
scenarios.desc: A question that is not a normal question
scenarios.setting: A table above the lake, two empty glasses, and a man at the next table already listening.

options.feedback: The safe answer, and he will ask again. Nobody in this canton is allowed to have no opinion on this.
An answer, said without hedging. It starts an argument and the argument is the point.
His answer. You will get forty minutes of agreement, which is less fun and perfectly pleasant.
Steiler, with er on the end. A comparative and a reason, which is what he asked for.

options.es: Der Pilatus ist besser als die Rigi.
options.feedback: Besser als is right and it is not a reason. He already knows what you think.
Then do not pick a side. Having one and not defending it is the worst of both.

steps.speaker: Timo
steps.es: Auf der Rigi kann meine Grossmutter laufen.
steps.en: My grandmother can walk on Rigi.

options.es: Das stimmt. Das ist ein Berg für Menschen.
options.en: That is true. That is a mountain for people.
options.feedback: Give him the point. He has been waiting to make it and it is a good one.

options.en: Mine could too, on the railway.
options.feedback: A joke back, at the same volume as his. That is how this argument is supposed to go.
It is his argument, and it is about his grandmother. Read the room.
He said two words to a table he is not at and then finished his beer. Nothing is required of you.

options.en: You see, I am on my own.
options.feedback: Fine and it invites him in. He was not asking to join, he was registering a vote.
He is not going to explain. He said the name of a mountain and that was the whole contribution.

scenarios.title: Nur wir zwei
scenarios.desc: Four hours, and you will remember three things
scenarios.setting: A flat mountain top, a path you can walk side by side, and nobody else along.

steps.speaker: Selina
steps.es: Was war dein erster Tag hier?
steps.en: What was your first day here like?

options.es: Vierzig Minuten am Flughafen ohne ein Wort.
options.en: Forty minutes at the airport without a word.
options.feedback: One concrete thing, not a summary. She asked for a day, so give her a day.
True and closed. Two adjectives are a lid, and she was opening something.
You do. It is the first question anybody has asked you that is not woher or seit wann.

steps.speaker: Selina
steps.es: Ich mag den Nebel lieber als die Sonne.
steps.en: I like fog better than sun.

options.feedback: One word, and you get ten minutes. Asking back is the whole skill here.
It is, and she knows. She said it because it is odd, and now she has to defend it.
You do not. Agreeing with something you have not thought about closes it faster than disagreeing.

steps.speaker: Selina
steps.es: Sollen wir noch eine Runde laufen?
steps.en: Shall we walk round once more?

options.feedback: One word. This is a mountain path, not a table: you walk side by side and you do not have to look at each other.
Honest. It is also the end of the afternoon, and she will not offer twice.
She asked what you want. Handing it back is the one answer with nothing in it.
Schön is a big word here. Matching it exactly is the answer; going bigger would put it back down.
A day, with no mal in it. That is the whole move and it is braver than it looks.

options.es: Das war der beste Tag seit Monaten!
options.en: That was the best day in months!
options.feedback: It may well have been. Said out loud at this volume it lands about three sizes too big.

scenarios.title: Ich mag dich
scenarios.desc: Three words with months between them
scenarios.setting: A train along the lake, a story about somebody on her ward, and the wrong moment.

steps.speaker: Selina
steps.es: Ich sitze jeden Abend zehn Minuten bei ihr.
steps.en: I sit with her for ten minutes every evening.

options.feedback: Ask. She is telling you something about herself and calling it a story about somebody else.
It is, and saying so turns her into somebody being praised. She will change the subject.
Not wrong, and not now. She is in the middle of something. Wait for the end of it.
Now. Ich mag dich is the small warm one and it is not small at all when it is said to a person.
Months too early. Here that word is an event, not a goodbye, and using it now spends it.
The step above. It sounds smaller in English and it is bigger in German.
Four seconds. Filling them would be the mistake: she is deciding what to do with what you said.
Now she has to manage your worry instead of her own answer. Let the silence finish.

options.en: You do not have to say anything.
options.feedback: Kind, and it takes the answer away from her. She was going to give you one.
She will go back to her story. Going back to the story is the biggest thing she can do: nothing is broken.
Yes. Asking makes her say it twice, and here nobody says anything twice.
Small and safe. It also closes something she just opened at some cost.

scenarios.title: Der erste Streit
scenarios.desc: Nobody raises their voice, which is worse
scenarios.setting: A kitchen on a Thursday, two cups, and a Saturday you did not mention.

options.feedback: The true answer and it costs you. Anything else here would be a second mistake on top of the first.
Vague where she was exact. Arguments here run on specifics, and blurring one is read as hiding it.
You did not. She is about to say so, and the difference between forgetting and not saying is the whole argument.
Schade is a very big word here. Explaining over the top of it is the second mistake.
Three minutes of explaining. She let you do it once and it did not help either of you.
Agreeing with the size of it. That is more than an apology and it takes four words.

steps.speaker: Selina
steps.es: Du hast es nicht vergessen. Du hast es nicht gesagt.
steps.en: You did not forget. You did not say it.

options.feedback: She is right. Forgetting is an accident and not saying is a small decision, and she named it exactly.

options.es: So habe ich das nicht gemeint.
options.en: I did not mean it that way.
options.feedback: The sentence for a misunderstanding, and this is not one. She will say doch.
It is not, and you know it is not. This is the point of the whole conversation.

steps.speaker: Selina
steps.en: I have to go to the hospital.

options.feedback: Fair, and it hands her the next move. Nothing was arranged and now nothing is.
A day. Leaving an argument with no date is the thing that makes two days feel like a month.
It is true that she is using it as a way out. It is also a night shift, and it starts at seven.

scenarios.title: Es tut mir leid
scenarios.desc: An apology has to name the thing
scenarios.setting: By the weir, loud enough that you both have to speak up, three days later than it should be.

options.es: Es tut mir leid für die zwei Tage.
options.en: I am sorry about the two days.
options.feedback: Sorry for what. A general es tut mir leid reads as evasion here; the thing has to be named.
She will wait. Not to punish you: she is waiting for the second half of the sentence.

options.en: I have thought about it a lot.
options.feedback: A good opening and not an apology. It is the sentence she uses, and she uses it before something.

options.es: Der Samstag war nicht das Problem.
options.en: The Saturday was not the problem.
options.feedback: Correct, and knowing which thing to apologise for is most of the work.

options.en: I am sorry about that too.
options.feedback: Adding items to the list is not the same as finding the right one.
She was. She was more right about the other thing, and that is what she is waiting for.

steps.speaker: Selina
steps.es: Ich war auch zu still. Ich mache das immer.
steps.en: I was too quiet too. I always do that.

options.feedback: Her own move, given back. Not ist schon gut, which would make what she just said smaller.
She did not offer it to be waved away. Letting it stand is the respectful thing here.
Warm and it does not shrink it. Slightly big for the register and it lands.
That is the end of it. No big sentence, no ceremony: a small ordinary thing done together.
Asking reopens it. Nobody here says the sentence that ends it, and Kaffee was the sentence.

options.es: Ja. Und dann muss ich noch etwas sagen.
options.en: Yes. And then I have one more thing to say.
options.feedback: If it is a new thing, fine. If it is the same thing again, it will undo the last half hour.

scenarios.title: Sonntagessen
scenarios.desc: Half past eleven to five, and the good plates
scenarios.setting: A house in Kriens from 1974, six pairs of shoes at the door, and a woman with wet hands.

options.feedback: Five minutes early is right and fifteen is a little much. Naming it yourself takes it off her.
Frau Odermatt, and Sie, and wait to be told otherwise. That may take a year.
Her first name, on the first Sunday, unasked. Here that is the one move you do not make.

steps.speaker: Marianne
steps.es: Sie sind also aus dem Süden.
steps.en: So you are from the south.

options.es: Ja. Aus einer kleinen Stadt am Meer.
options.en: Yes. From a small town by the sea.
options.feedback: One more sentence than the question needed. That is the opening move and she will take it.
Correct and closed. She has thirty-nine more questions and now they all have to be hers.
Selina told her, three weeks ago, in detail. Everybody at this table knows more than they say.

steps.speaker: Kurt
steps.es: Wie ist das Wasser bei Ihnen?
steps.en: What is the water like where you come from?

options.es: Man kann es trinken. Es schmeckt nach nichts.
options.en: You can drink it. It tastes of nothing.
options.feedback: He is asking whether you can drink from the tap. It is his first question about any country.
Fair. He will not rephrase it, he will wait, and you will work it out in the silence.
He has asked you two questions in three hours. This is one of them.

options.es: Das ist eine gute Frage. Da muss ich noch schauen.
options.en: That is a good question. I still have to look into that.
options.feedback: The polite deflection, twice over. Nobody asks again, and nobody is offended.
Pay is private here. The pension is not, and neither is rent. The line sits somewhere else.
Honest, and she will now explain all three pillars over the roast. Which is not the worst outcome.

scenarios.title: Mein Deutsch ist heute schlecht
scenarios.desc: The kindness that makes it worse
scenarios.setting: The same table, a bad night's sleep, and nine people talking at ordinary speed.

steps.speaker: Marianne
steps.es: Und was machen Sie beruflich, also genau?
steps.en: And what do you do for work, exactly?

options.es: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
options.en: How do you say that in German?
options.feedback: A question, not a weakness. It is the single most useful sentence in the language.

options.es: Also. Ich mache... Zahlen und Briefe.
options.en: So. I do... numbers and letters.
